result: The MB lobes comprise approximately 2200 neurons consisting of 7 KC types, 21 MBON types (34 individual MBONs), and 20 DAN types (over 100 individual DANs). This comprehensive census was achieved through split-GAL4 screening and PA-GFP tracing.
evaluation: Claims C61, C28, C82, and C94 collectively establish the complete neuronal composition of the MB lobes. The findings are supported by multiple complementary methods (split-GAL4 lines, PA-GFP tracing, cell counting) that converge on consistent numbers. The near-saturation of the screen (C73) and validation through independent approaches (C76, C77, C80) provide strong evidence for completeness.

result: The 21 MBON types elaborate segregated dendritic arbors that form 15 compartments collectively tiling the MB lobes with minimal overlap. This compartmentalization was demonstrated through computational alignment and validated by two-color labeling experiments.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C62, C102-C104, and C106 describe the compartmental organization of MBON dendrites with converging evidence from computational alignment (C104) and experimental validation (C106). The segregation is clearly demonstrated in Figures 10 and 11, with quantitative assessment showing minimal overlap between adjacent compartments.

result: Each of the 20 DAN types projects axons to one or at most two MBON compartments, with DAN axon terminals tiling the entire MB lobes. This compartmentalized organization matches the MBON dendritic compartments.
evaluation: Claims C6, C63, C114, C115, and C118 establish the compartmentalized projection pattern of DANs. The evidence includes split-GAL4 driver lines, photoactivation experiments, and computational alignment (Figure 10). The tiling pattern and segregation are validated through two-color labeling (C116, C117), providing strong anatomical evidence.

result: The alignment of DAN axons with compartmentalized KC-MBON synapses creates isolated units for learning that can transform the disordered KC representation into ordered MBON output, with specific dopaminergic input capable of modifying synapses between KCs and specific MBONs.
evaluation: Claims C7, C64, C119, C121, C183, and C185 make functional inferences about learning mechanisms based on anatomical organization. While the anatomical compartmentalization is well-supported, the functional claims about learning transformation are speculative and require physiological validation. The manuscript provides anatomical substrate but not direct evidence of the proposed learning mechanisms.

result: MBON axons project to five discrete neuropils outside the MB: the crepine (CRE), superior medial protocerebrum (SMP), superior intermediate protocerebrum (SIP), superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP), and lateral horn (LH), with most MBON types projecting to several of these regions.
evaluation: Claims C4, C65, C141, C142, and C198 describe MBON output projections supported by computational alignment of axon terminals (Figure 18). The identification of five discrete target neuropils is well-documented with quantitative analysis showing 99% of MBON terminals distributed in these regions (C18E). The methodology is sound and results are internally consistent.

result: Three MBON types (MBON-γ4>γ1γ2, MBON-β1>α, and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β) project axons back into the MB lobes, forming a multi-layered feedforward network where information flows unidirectionally without feedback to the originating compartment.
evaluation: Claims C5, C123-C125, and C189 describe feedforward connections within the MB supported by anatomical tracing (Figure 17). The unidirectional flow is demonstrated by showing that MBONs project to other compartments but not back to their own dendritic compartments. The evidence is clear and well-documented, though functional implications remain to be tested.

result: The α1, α2, and α3 MBONs represent a four-layer feedforward network with access to KC activity from both α/β and γ lobes, which may support more sophisticated neuronal computations than the simpler one- and two-layer systems in other lobes.
evaluation: Claims C133, C138, C190, and C191 describe a four-layer network architecture based on anatomical connectivity (Figure 17). While the anatomical organization is well-documented (C133 is SUPPORTED), the functional claims about computational sophistication (C138, C190, C191) are speculative, relying on machine learning principles rather than experimental evidence. The computational advantages require physiological validation.

result: Ninety percent of DAN dendritic arbors reside in four neuropils (CRE, SMP, SIP, SLP) that also receive MBON axon terminals, suggesting these are convergence zones for unconditioned stimulus (US) input and sites where all signals relevant for classical conditioning converge.
evaluation: Claims C147 and C200 describing the anatomical overlap are well-supported by computational alignment (Figures 18-19). However, claims C148, C199, and C201 about US input and classical conditioning convergence are inferences based on prior functional studies rather than direct evidence from this work. The anatomical substrate is established, but functional validation is needed.

result: MBON terminals overlap with DAN dendrites within convergence neuropils, creating potential feedback loops where MBONs may synapse on DANs that modulate either the same compartment or different compartments, enabling recurrent modulation of learning.
evaluation: Claim C150 describing anatomical overlap is supported by computational alignment (Figure 20). However, claims C151, C152, C193, and C197 about functional feedback and modulation are speculative. The manuscript shows spatial proximity but does not demonstrate actual synaptic connections or functional interactions. Electron microscopy or physiological studies would be needed to confirm these proposed circuits.

result: Five KC types that receive olfactory information (γmain, α′/β′ap, α′/β′m, α/βc, α/βs) are each represented by hundreds of neurons with dendrites in the main calyx, and each type sends axonal projections to spatially segregated layers in the lobes, though dendritic zones overlap and individual KCs show variable dendritic patterns.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 describe KC organization supported by split-GAL4 driver lines, cell counting, and anatomical analysis (Figures 6-7). The segregated axonal layers are clearly demonstrated, and the overlapping dendritic zones with individual variability are documented through single-cell analysis. The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent.

result: MBONs using the same neurotransmitter extend dendrites to adjacent regions of the lobes: cholinergic MBONs in vertical lobes (α and α′), glutamatergic MBONs in medial lobes (β, β′, γ), and GABAergic MBONs at the intersection between these regions.
evaluation: Claims C96 and C85 describe neurotransmitter-based spatial organization supported by immunostaining for neurotransmitter markers (Figure 9). The segregation of different transmitter types to specific lobe regions is clearly demonstrated with appropriate antibody controls. The methodology is sound and results are well-documented.

result: The convergence of approximately 2000 KCs onto only 34 MBONs (21 cell types) transforms the high-dimensional KC representation into a low-dimensional MBON output, suggesting MBONs encode state variables that bias behavioral responses rather than representing odor identity.
evaluation: Claims C111, C173, and C174 about the dimensional transformation are logical inferences based on the established neuronal counts. However, claim C175 about MBONs encoding state variables rather than odor identity is speculative. While the anatomical convergence is well-documented, the functional interpretation requires physiological recordings of MBON responses to validate the proposed coding scheme.

result: A comprehensive screen of 7000 GAL4 lines followed by generation and screening of 2500 split-GAL4 intersections yielded over 400 split-GAL4 combinations with strong MB expression, with an average of 12 GAL4 drivers per cell type indicating near-saturation of the screen.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 and C73 describe the screening methodology and its completeness. The near-saturation conclusion (C73) is supported by the finding that multiple independent drivers label the same cell types. The convergence of split-GAL4 and PA-GFP approaches (C76, C80) provides additional validation of completeness.

result: PA-GFP photoactivation experiments independently validated the split-GAL4 results, with photoactivation of MB lobes labeling eight individual neurons and five clusters matching split-GAL4 findings, plus revealing two additional MBONs not in the split-GAL4 collection.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 and C80 describe PA-GFP validation experiments (Figures 4-5). The convergence between split-GAL4 and PA-GFP approaches provides strong evidence for completeness, while the identification of two additional MBONs (C78, C79) demonstrates the complementary nature of the methods. The methodology is well-described with appropriate controls.

result: Single-cell analysis revealed that members of each MBON type exhibit indistinguishable morphology with stereotyped projection patterns that are invariant across individual flies, and most split-GAL4 lines contain small numbers of bilaterally symmetric neurons with virtually identical morphologies.
evaluation: Claims C100, C101, C69, and C72 describe the stereotypy of MBON morphology supported by multicolor flp-out experiments and analysis across multiple individuals. The consistency across flies is well-documented in the figures and supplementary materials. This stereotypy contrasts with KC variability and supports the operational definition of cell types.

result: Among the 21 MBON types, 13 extend dendrites to a single compartment while 8 project to two compartments, and most innervate all KC layers within a compartment though eight types restrict dendrites to specific layers.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 describe MBON dendritic organization supported by anatomical analysis (Figures 11-12). The compartment and layer specificity is clearly documented through split-GAL4 lines and two-color labeling. The data are comprehensive and internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches.

result: Within each target neuropil, MBON axon terminals exhibit distinct and confined projection patterns suggesting different postsynaptic targets, though significant overlap between some MBON types suggests potential convergence onto common postsynaptic neurons.
evaluation: Claims C143-C145 describe MBON terminal organization supported by computational alignment (Figures 19-20) and validated by two-color labeling (C145). The methodology appropriately distinguishes between segregated and overlapping projections. However, the inference about postsynaptic targets (C143, C144) requires electron microscopy or other connectivity methods for confirmation.

result: Four MBON types project to the lateral horn, a region responsible for innate odor responses, potentially allowing learned responses to exploit circuits for innate behaviors or to modulate innate responses through learning.
evaluation: Claim C154 about four MBONs projecting to LH is supported by anatomical data (Figure 18). Claim C155 about LH mediating innate responses is well-established knowledge. However, claims C156 and C157 about exploiting innate circuits or modulating innate responses are speculative inferences requiring functional validation through behavioral or physiological experiments.

result: KCs comprise 2000 neurons defining only seven cell types that receive unstructured inputs and connect to multiple MBONs through plastic synapses, affording the MB the ability to contextualize novel sensory experiences consistent with its role in learned behavior.
evaluation: Claim C164 about seven KC types is well-supported by the current study. Claims C165 and C166 about unstructured inputs and plastic synapses are supported by cited prior work. However, claim C167 about contextualizing novel experiences is an inference that, while reasonable, extends beyond the anatomical data presented and requires functional validation.

result: The KC representation has a dimension at least an order of magnitude larger than the antennal lobe due to greater KC numbers and nonlinear mixing of inputs, with features (lack of structure, small input number, sparse activity) tuned to maximize this dimension, optimizing the fly's ability to contextualize olfactory experiences.
evaluation: Claims C169-C172 make theoretical arguments about dimensionality and optimization based on cited prior work and computational principles. While the logic is sound and supported by citations (C169, C171), these are inferences rather than direct experimental findings of the current study. The optimization claims (C171, C172) require additional theoretical or experimental validation.

result: The convergence zones (CRE, SMP, SIP, SLP) may represent an evolutionary primitive circuit where US inputs activate motor command neurons for innate responses, with MB pathways later incorporated to generate learned behaviors, potentially utilizing fan-shaped body projecting neurons that arborize in these zones.
evaluation: Claims C205 and C206 are speculative evolutionary hypotheses without direct supporting evidence. Claims C203 and C204 about fan-shaped body connections are supported by citations but don't directly validate the evolutionary scenario. Claim C202 about motor commands is an inference. This is an interesting hypothesis but requires comparative neuroanatomical or functional evidence for validation.

result: The MB diverges from typical invertebrate neural architecture with its large number of equivalent neurons (KCs) that increase with behavioral complexity and receive non-stereotyped inputs, potentially representing an evolutionary primitive structure homologous to vertebrate brain structures.
evaluation: Claims C209-C213 about MB diverging from typical invertebrate organization are supported by the current anatomical findings and general knowledge. Claim C211 about KC numbers increasing with complexity is supported by citation (C211). However, claim C214 about homology to vertebrate structures is highly speculative, based on superficial similarities rather than rigorous comparative or evolutionary analysis.

result: One DAN type (PAM-γ4<γ1γ2) that projects to γ4 extends dendrites to γ1 and γ2 compartments where they appear to receive direct inputs from MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 axon terminals, creating a recurrent loop involving modulatory dopamine input.
evaluation: Claim C134 about DAN dendrites in γ1 and γ2 is supported by anatomical tracing (Figure 17). However, claim C135 that dendrites 'appear to receive direct inputs' from MBON terminals is based on spatial proximity rather than demonstrated synaptic connectivity. The recurrent loop is inferred from anatomy but requires electron microscopy or physiological validation to confirm functional connections.

result: The split-GAL4 collection identified approximately 30% fewer PAM cluster DANs compared to PA-GFP and anti-dopamine immunoreactivity estimates, with the additional DANs exhibiting similar innervation patterns suggesting they represent closely related cell types or reflect stochastic driver expression.
evaluation: Claims C83 and C84 acknowledge a discrepancy between methods and provide reasonable explanations. The comparison between split-GAL4 (98 DANs) and PA-GFP/immunostaining (115-135 DANs) is quantitatively documented (Figure 5). The interpretation that missing cells represent related types or stochastic expression is reasonable given the similar innervation patterns observed.

result: MBON cell types vary in cell number per hemisphere: 14 types consist of one cell, six types contain two cells, and one type contains eight cells per hemisphere.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 describe MBON cell numbers supported by split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting. The data are clearly presented in Table 1 and figures. The methodology for cell counting is appropriate, and the consistency across individuals (mentioned in C101) supports the reliability of these counts.

result: DAN types from the PPL1 cluster contain one or two cells per hemisphere while PAM cluster DAN types contain up to approximately 20 cells per hemisphere.
evaluation: Claim C113 describes DAN cell numbers supported by split-GAL4 driver lines and cell counting (Table 1, Figures 14-16). The methodology is consistent with that used for MBONs. The discrepancy with PA-GFP counts (C83) is acknowledged and explained, providing transparency about the limitations.

result: Ensheathing glia are present at borders between MB lobes but not between MBON compartments within each lobe.
evaluation: Claim C107 is supported by two-color labeling experiments showing glia at lobe boundaries but not compartment boundaries (Figure 11J-L). This finding is clearly documented with appropriate imaging and provides insight into the structural organization of compartments versus lobes. The methodology is straightforward and results are unambiguous.

result: Computational alignment reveals gaps between MBON dendritic arbors at four compartment borders, which correspond to areas of reduced synaptic density as shown by Bruchpilot staining.
evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by computational alignment (Figure 10) and validated by presynaptic marker staining (Figure 10—figure supplement 1). The correlation between anatomical gaps and reduced synaptic density provides functional insight into compartment boundaries. The methodology appropriately combines computational and experimental approaches.
